domains.name: Deep Learning Foundations and Theory
domains.summary: The mathematical and algorithmic core that makes neural networks trainable: how gradient-based fitting of deep parameterized functions works, why initialization/normalization/optimization choices determine trainability, and what theory actually says about expressivity, generalization, and the infinite-width limit. This domain supplies the primitives every architecture, generative model, and vision system in the other domains is built from.

subdomains.name: Network Expressivity, Depth, and History
subdomains.summary: Where the modern network came from and what depth buys: approximation capacity versus practical representation learning.

topics.name: From Perceptron to Multilayer Networks
topics.definition: The perceptron is a linear threshold unit computing sign(w.x + b); stacking units into layers with nonlinear activations and training them by gradient descent gives the multilayer network that modern deep learning generalizes.
topics.explanation: Rosenblatt's 1958 perceptron solved only linearly separable problems, and Minsky and Papert's 1969 analysis of parity and XOR limits caused first-generation funding to collapse; the same argument, restated geometrically, is that a single threshold layer partitions input space with one hyperplane. The 1986 backpropagation line (Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams), building on Linnainmaa's 1970 reverse-mode autodiff and Werbos's 1974 thesis, made multilayer weights trainable and triggered the second wave, which was then crowded out in the 1990s by kernel methods and pushed out of vision/ASR by 2006-2012 by GPU-trained deep nets (LeCun's LeNet and convnets, Hinton's greedy layerwise pretraining, Krizhevsky's AlexNet). Two lessons from this history are still load-bearing: universal approximation says capacity was never the bottleneck, so what changed trainability was data, computation, gradient-based optimization, and better activations/normalization; and every past 'deep learning winter' was a failure of optimization scale, not of the model class. Learning this lineage also fixes terminology: 'deep' means many composed nonlinear layers, 'shallow' nets with one hidden layer remain universal approximators and are still used.
learning_objectives: State the decision boundary a single perceptron implements and prove it cannot represent XOR.
Explain why the 1969 limitations paper did not refute multilayer capability.
Order the key enabling events (reverse-mode autodiff, backprop, GPUs, AlexNet) by what each unlocked.
Implement a single-layer perceptron learning rule and demonstrate its failure on non-separable data.
applications: Understanding why 'deep' is an optimization claim
common_misconceptions: The perceptron is a multilayer network (Rosenblatt's original was a single trained layer plus fixed random preprocessing).
XOR proves perceptrons are useless rather than proving one layer is insufficient.
Deep learning replaced classical AI because it is more accurate in principle (it replaced it because of scale and feature learning).

topics.name: Universal Approximation, Depth Separation, and Representation Learning
topics.definition: Universal approximation theorems state that a single hidden layer with enough width can approximate any continuous function on a compact domain; depth separation results state that some functions need exponentially many more neurons if depth is removed.
topics.explanation: Cybenko (sigmoidal), Hornik (squashing, arbitrary open sets) and later Barron, Kurkova and Leshno established density, not efficiency: the theorems are silent about how many units, what weights, or how to find them by gradient descent, and the required width typically grows exponentially with input dimension and target accuracy. Depth-aware results are what make networks interesting: Telgarsky's sawtooth construction gives functions realized by O(depth) networks that need width exponential in depth for any shallow net; Eldan-Shamir separate Gaussian mixtures; Raina et al. give a complexity-theoretic separation for strongly polynomial oracle functions; Safran-Shamir show depth can help for some functions and hurt for others, so 'depth is always better' is false. The practical view is representation learning: each layer performs a learned feature map, and composition allows reuse of intermediate features so that a function factored into subfunctions needs far fewer parameters when the factorization is exposed. This is why deep nets on images/sequences do not need the astronomical widths the density theorems suggest, and why the relevant quantity is approximation rate as a function of parameter count (Barron's O(s/sqrt(n)) bound for targets with integrable spectral moment), plus the inductive bias of the architecture and optimizer. A learner should be able to say precisely what the theorems do and do not license.

subdomains.name: Gradients and Automatic Differentiation
subdomains.summary: Backpropagation treated as the algorithm it is: reverse-mode automatic differentiation, with the forward/reverse distinction and JVP/VJP primitives that most courses skip.

topics.name: Backpropagation as Reverse-Mode Automatic Differentiation
topics.definition: Backpropagation is reverse-mode automatic differentiation applied to the scalar loss of a computation graph: gradients are accumulated by composing vector-Jacobian products backward through layers, cost O(#primitives) times the forward cost.
topics.explanation: Griewank's 1989 thesis formalized the two modes. If y = F(x) in R^m with Jacobian J, forward mode propagates tangent vectors v -> J v (a Jacobian-vector product, JVP) and costs O(n) passes to get the full Jacobian, so it is efficient when inputs outnumber outputs; reverse mode propagates covectors u -> u^T J (a vector-Jacobian product, VJP) and costs O(m) passes, so it is efficient when a scalar (loss) depends on many parameters, which is exactly the deep learning regime. Backprop is therefore not 'the chain rule' as folklore says but an efficient schedule for a composition of VJPs, with the number of operations in a reverse pass essentially equal to the forward pass because the required intermediates were cached in the tape. Gelfand-Yaglom's 1963 reverse formulation and Linnainmaa's 1970 accumulation of adjoint derivatives are the true ancestors; Baydin et al.'s tutorial is the standard modern derivation. A practitioner must be able to derive VJPs for the primitives that cause most real bugs: matmul (dX = dY B^T, dB = X^T dY), reductions and broadcasting (sum-backward is broadcast; axis bookkeeping is where silent errors live), softmax plus cross-entropy (dL/dz = p - y), layernorm, convolution (a transposed-correlation), and in-place ops/aliases that break tape assumptions. Differentiation of a network trained with weight tying, dropout, or non-differentiable sampling requires care (straight-through estimators, score-function alternatives), and gradient accumulation is just VJP linearity exploited across microbatches.
learning_objectives: State the JVP and VJP of a scalar-valued and a vector-valued function and explain which mode is cheaper for loss-on-many-parameters.

subdomains.name: Optimization and Trainability
subdomains.summary: The practical and theoretical machinery that decides whether a deep network can be fit: initializers, normalization, optimizers, schedules, and the pathology of gradient magnitudes.

topics.name: Optimization for Neural Networks: SGD, Adaptive Methods, and Schedules
topics.definition: The family of first-order updates used to fit deep networks - minibatch SGD, momentum and Nesterov, AdaGrad/RMSProp/Adam/AdamW, large-batch methods (LARS/LAMB), and Lion - together with the learning-rate schedule and warmup that make them usable.
topics.explanation: Deep learning optimization is nonconvex, noisy (finite minibatches), high-dimensional, badly conditioned, and often ill-behaved at the boundary (weight-norm-driven losses), so convex-analysis guarantees rarely transfer. Minibatch SGD with momentum exploits gradient correlation across steps and implicitly low-pass filters noise; Nesterov's look-ahead gives a modest improvement and better accelerated-method interpretation. AdaGrad accumulates squared gradients (adaptive, subgradient-friendly, eventually stalls), RMSProp exponentially averages them, and Adam combines momentum with an exponential moving average of squared gradients, adding bias correction and a decoupled epsilon placement that matters at fp16. AdamW removes the coupling defect where L2 regularization is diluted by the adaptive denominator, which is why decoupled weight decay is now the default. For very large batches the critical-batch-size idea (You, Mishkin) plus layer-wise adaptive rates (LARS) or trust ratios (LAMB) with linear scaling of LR to batch size and warmup makes thousand-GPU runs converge; Lion is a sign-of-interpolated-gradient method with outer momentum that trades memory for an extra forward and behaves like an Adam variant with weight-decoupled signs. Schedules: warmup stabilizes second-moment estimates and prevents the early large-step blowup; cosine/linear decay approximate annealing; the LR-noise scale (McCandlish's batch size and LR should scale together; gradient noise scale measures how far from a big-step regime you are). Also worth teaching honestly: adaptive methods are not universally better than well-tuned SGD+momentum (Wilson et al.'s diagnostic task analysis; Adam can be worse on some convex/ill-conditioned problems, and AMSGrad's fix is empirically marginal), and optimizer choice interacts with normalization (bias correction after layernorm) and with weight decay effective through Adam's scaling.

topics.name: Gradient Pathologies, Signal Propagation, and Initialization Theory
topics.definition: Vanishing and exploding gradients are the failure of gradient magnitudes to remain order-one through depth; initialization theory derives weight scales (Xavier, He, and modern mean-field/residual-aware variants) that keep forward activations and backward gradients critically scaled.
topics.explanation: In a naive L-layer network, layer-to-layer Jacobians multiply, so pre-activation variances scale like prod_l (n_l Var(w_l) E[phi'(z_l)^2]): if the per-layer gain is <1 activations collapse toward the mean (the signal dies and the top layers see no information), if >1 activations saturate in sigmoid tails or overflow and gradients explode. The same factor appears transposed in the backward pass, which is why a single design principle - keep the forward/backward gain near 1 at every layer, in expectation over the data and the random weights - governs initialization. Xavier/Glorot sets Var(w) = 2/(n_in+n_out) for symmetric saturating activations; He/Kaiming sets Var(w) = 2/n_in for ReLU (half the units are zero); the fan-in convention and whether gain includes the activation derivative (and convolution's spatial support) are the usual sources of off-by-sqrt(2) errors. Beyond variance matching: dropout changes effective gain; normalization layers change it again (a properly normalized network is nearly insensitive to init scale - the 'residual branch' exception, where scaled init of residual outputs, e.g. zero-init on LayerScale or Fixup's scheme, keeps the network near identity at start). The mean-field/NTK view says init also selects which regime training lives in (lazy vs feature-learning), and muP makes hyperparameters (LR, momentum, init std, Adam eps) transferable between a small proxy model and the full one by scaling them with width - the single most practically valuable init-related idea. Also teach the numerical side: exploding gradients in fp16, gradient clipping by global norm as a (biased but stabilizing) projection, and the different failure of dead-ReLU collapse.

topics.name: Normalization Layers: Batch, Layer, Group, Instance, RMSNorm
topics.definition: Normalization layers are differentiable, parameterized functions that rescale and shift activations over chosen tensor axes - batch statistics for BatchNorm, per-example feature statistics for LayerNorm, channel groups, spatial statistics for InstanceNorm, and an RMS-only rescale for RMSNorm.
topics.explanation: The unifying formula is: given a tensor, compute a mean and variance over an axis set A (BatchNorm: A = batch and often spatial axes; LayerNorm: A = feature dim; GroupNorm: A = (C/G) features per group; InstanceNorm: A = spatial per channel), then z = (x - mu)/sqrt(sigma^2 + eps) * gamma + beta. BatchNorm additionally maintains running estimates used at inference and creates the train/eval discrepancy plus a batch-size dependence that breaks small-batch and stateful/online settings - and its coupling of examples inside a minibatch is why it interacts badly with sequence models and with data parallelism (needing synchronized statistics). LayerNorm removes cross-example dependence, which is what makes autoregressive and per-token normalization coherent; RMSNorm drops mean-centering and uses the root-mean-square scale, which is cheaper and empirically equivalent in LLMs, and modern LLMs apply it before each block. Normalization placement is a first-order design question: post-norm x_{l+1} = LN(x_l + f(x_l)) trains stably only to modest depth, while pre-norm x_{l+1} = x_l + LN(f(x_l)) removes the multiplicative residual growth (identity is not rescaled each block) so very deep models train, at the cost of a weaker residual signal, an effectively smaller 'depth budget', and the need for final normalization; DeepNorm, sandwich/normalized-LN and Yarn-style scalings are attempts to get both. Theories of normalization are genuinely contested: the internal-covariate-shift story of the original BatchNorm paper is not well supported, and the better-supported accounts are Lipschitz/smoothness of the loss, gradient variance reduction, and reparameterization of the scale so effective learning rate and weight decay decouple from activation magnitude - the last explains why a normalized network's optimum has a well-defined direction and why weight norm alone does not change the function, which is also why LayerNorm models need decoupled weight decay.

topics.name: Activation Functions and Their Mathematics
topics.definition: The scalar nonlinearity applied elementwise to pre-activations; its derivative shape, saturation, monotonicity, zero-mean-ness, and smoothness determine gradient flow, approximation class, and optimization behavior.
topics.explanation: Sigmoid and tanh are bounded, saturated, and have derivative <= 1/4 and <= 1 respectively, which multiplicatively attenuates gradients with depth and pushes pre-activations into flat regions - tanh's zero mean is a real advantage over sigmoid for centered data. ReLU removed saturation on the positive side, kept sparse (partly zero-mean-breaking) activations, is piecewise linear so the network computes a continuous piecewise-linear function with a combinatorial region count exponential in depth, and introduced the dying-unit problem when mean pre-activations are negative; leaky/PReLU/ELU/SELU variants trade back saturation for zero-mean-ness (SELU comes with a self-normalizing fixed point under dropout assumptions, which is why it demands specific init). Smooth functions matter more than they look: GELU is x*Phi(x) - a probabilistic gate that became the transformer default - and Swish/SiLU is x*sigmoid(bx), both nonmonotone with bounded negative dips, which softens optimization and interacts with attention entropy; SiLU/GELU are preferred where the model must be differentiable everywhere (second-order methods, curvature regularizers) while ReLU's nondifferentiability is a measure-zero annoyance in practice. Also worth covering: why bounded activations cap attention logits' effect, why softmax/tanh choices change information geometry, and the practical question of choosing activation with the normalization/init scheme jointly rather than as a hyperparameter afterthought. Include the 'which nonlinearity can the network approximate well' framing: piecewise-linear nets are universal on compact sets, and smooth nonmonotone nets change region-count and spectral-bias properties (ReLU has a spectral bias toward low frequencies, affecting where it fits noise).

topics.name: Regularization for Deep Networks: Weight Decay, Dropout, Augmentation, Label Smoothing
topics.definition: Techniques that reduce generalization gap without changing the model class: penalty terms (L2/weight decay), stochastic unit masking (dropout), input-target transformations (augmentation), and target smoothing (label smoothing, mixup).
topics.explanation: Weight decay added to the loss is ridge regularization in parameter space, biasing toward smaller-norm, flatter, better-conditioned solutions; in adaptive optimizers the penalty's effective strength is rescaled by the preconditioner, hence decoupled weight decay (AdamW). Crucially, for scale-invariant parameterizations (normed layers, homogeneous activations) pure L2 does not change the function it only changes effective step size, so weight decay's regularization value must be understood via the induced effective LR and margin rather than raw capacity. Dropout trains an implicit ensemble by sampling Bernoulli masks at unit level; its standard test-time rescaling is an approximation to the exponential ensemble, and its regularizing effect is variance/noise injection plus implicit input-gradient regularization, while it is rarely used in modern LLMs (where it hurts at scale) and still used for encoder-decoder hidden states. Data augmentation is regularization in function space via a prior on invariances, and the strongest versions are systematic (RandAugment, AutoAugment learned by policy, MixUp/CutMix as convex interpolation and its implicit distributional-smoothness regularization). Label smoothing changes the target to (1-eps)y + eps/K, which primarily (a) softens gradients from overconfident logits, (b) improves calibration in the CE-optimal distribution sense, (c) acts as an entropy maximizer - and in vision transformers, where attention logits saturate easily, eps about 0.1 is standard. Also include the modern reality: dropout and weight decay trade off against batch size and augmentation strength, and 'regularization' now often means early stopping, EMA of weights, mixup-family interpolation, and explicit noise, which is why it belongs next to the loss-landscape topic rather than classical statistics.

subdomains.name: Depth as Dynamics and Limit Theory
subdomains.summary: Viewpoints that treat trained networks as dynamical systems and as objects with asymptotic regimes: residual nets as discretized ODEs, neural ODEs, and the infinite-width (NTK/mean-field) picture.

topics.name: Residual Connections, Network-as-ODE, and Neural ODEs
topics.definition: A residual block writes x_{l+1} = x_l + h f(x_l), i.e. one Euler step of an ODE dx/dt = f(x); viewing depth as time makes the network a discretized dynamical system and lets the ODE be learned continuously (neural ODEs, adjoint backpropagation).
topics.explanation: The Euler-step reading is exact with h = 1/L: as depth grows at fixed total integration length, a residual network converges to a continuous-depth flow generated by the learned vector field, which explains (a) why plain networks explode (each layer multiplies instead of adding, so log-norm grows linearly and identity is unobtainable), (b) why extremely deep residual nets train (the identity path preserves gradient magnitude, and the block functions can be small), (c) why the ensemble-of-paths picture (Veit et al.) works - variable-length paths with skipping, and (d) why scaling residual branches (zero/LayerScale/Fixup) matters. From there the ODE becomes the model: neural ODEs parameterize f with a network and integrate with an adaptive solver, so depth is continuous, and the backward pass uses the adjoint sensitivity method of Pontryagin - solve the augmented ODE for a(x) = dL/dx backwards, giving O(depth)-free memory at the cost of extra integration and possible numerical instability. Extensions worth teaching: continuous normalization flows (invertible, ODE-based generative models), ANODEs, GANs/flow-matching as vector-field learning, Hamiltonian and symplectic networks where conserved structure is imposed, latent-dynamics world models, and control interpretation via the residual-as-learned-controllers framing (Paul Chang's 'functional residual networks' essay). Honest limits: adjoint gradients are less exact than a discrete backward pass, adaptive solvers and stiffness cause training pathologies, and in practice continuous-depth nets have not beaten discrete residual nets at scale - the ODE view is best understood as a design and analysis lens (also the correct frame for understanding depth-scaling instabilities and the 'rank collapse' of plain deep nets).

topics.name: Infinite-Width Limit: Neural Tangent Kernel and Mean-Field View
topics.definition: Under a specific scaling of outputs and learning rate, a wide network's training converges to kernel regression with the Neural Tangent Kernel (frozen features, no representation learning), while the alternative mean-field scaling describes gradient flow as movement of the empirical distribution of neurons.
topics.explanation: Jacot et al. showed that with output scaled by 1/width and infinitesimal LR, a network's parameters move little, so the dynamics linearize around initialization: the training function evolves by gradient descent in the RKHS induced by Theta(x,x') = <g(x), g(x')> where g = grad_theta f(x); at infinite width the kernel is analytic (for ReLU, a closed-form arcsine-kernel composition over layers), fixed, and the solution is kernel regression - provably no feature learning, and empirically worse than finite-width training on compositional/label-heavy tasks. The NTK is genuinely useful: it gives the cleanest available theory of generalization and of 'which functions are learned fast' (spectral bias: components with large kernel eigenvalues fit first, explaining the low-frequency preference), it justifies muP and init/width scaling rules (the NTK parametrization is one of the two muP regimes), and it supplies a rigorous language for discussing how far from lazy a real model is. Chizat and Bach's distinction names the other limit: in the mean-field parametrization (second layer weights scaled by 1/m, i.e. 'maximal' or mean-field scaling), gradient flow is a Wasserstein gradient flow on the neuron measure, the limiting object is a distribution over neurons rather than a fixed kernel, and the dynamics provably can learn features - with mean-field analyses giving global convergence for two-layer nets under assumptions (Mei-Montenegro-NG, Rotskoff-Vanden-Eijnden, Nitanda-Suzuki) and the notable result that feature-learning scaling yields better-than-kernel rates. The empirical status is the pedagogically important part: real trained networks are measurably NTK-different (kernel alignment studies: NTK predictions often beat the trained net on some tasks and lose on others, and 'beyond-NTK' corrections explain part of the gap), so neither limit describes practice; both are, however, the correct framework for reasoning about width scaling, LR transfer, and whether a loss curve represents feature learning at all.

topics.name: Loss Landscapes, Flat Minima, Double Descent, and Grokking
topics.definition: Phenomena about the geometry of deep loss surfaces and the training trajectory: flat-versus-sharp minima and their empirical link to generalization, the double-descent risk curve across the interpolation threshold, and grokking where generalization emerges long after memorization.
topics.explanation: Sharpness intuitions (high loss curvature/Hessian trace or large loss-basin width should hurt test performance) motivated SAM and flatness-seeking training and do correlate in practice within an architecture, but the classical mathematical story 'flatness causes generalization' is not clean: scaling by a constant can make any sharp minimum arbitrarily flat without changing the function (a fact that breaks naive norm-based sharpness definitions unless the flatness is measured with a scale-invariant notion such as relative curvature or normalized margin), and deep nets have degenerate directions where the Hessian is zero regardless of solution quality. Empirically the Hessian spectrum is heavy-tailed with a bulk of small eigenvalues and a few large ones; loss surfaces in the same basin are connected by low-barrier paths for over-parameterized nets (mode connectivity), which suggests single-basin training. Double descent reframes the classical U-curve: as parameter count approaches n the model can interpolate the labels exactly, the risk of classical estimators blows up near that threshold (variance of the interpolating solution), and then decreases again as further over-parameterization makes the minimum-norm interpolator implicit - observed for nets, and proven in linear/kernel settings, though 'benign overfitting' depends strongly on data geometry (random-label double descent is weaker). Grokking is the delayed-generalization phenomenon on algorithmic tasks (modular arithmetic, boolean/cobalt-style synthetic data): near-zero train error with test error ~0.5 for long training, then a sharp transition to generalization. Current best accounts are optimization/regularization rather than capacity: weight decay (plus long training and small data) drives the model to a structured, low-complexity solution; ablation of components (attention vs MLP) suggests a memorizing circuit is first found then replaced by an algorithmic circuit; phase-transition language and 'grokking as delayed margin/RBM-like regularization' have all appeared. It is genuinely open whether grokking transfers to real tasks, and its practical lesson is: do not stop training at the point of zero train loss, and treat test-accuracy curves with an explicit 'delayed generalization' hypothesis.

topics.name: Convolutional Networks: Operators, Receptive Fields, and the Architecture Lineage
topics.definition: A convolutional layer applies a small shared linear filter across spatial positions with local connectivity and translation equivariance; a convolutional architecture is a hierarchy of such layers plus pooling, normalization and nonlinearities, whose design history is a sequence of answers to the depth-and-cost problem.
topics.explanation: Discrete convolution (correlation in framework terms) maps an input feature map X in R^{CxHxW} to output channels by summing over a k x k spatial window and all input channels, giving C_out parameters per layer independent of resolution - this is the parameter-sharing prior that makes images tractable, and it buys exact translation equivariance (with padding and pooling, approximate invariance). Receptive field grows additively per stacked kxK layer and multiplicatively with stride, so the effective field of a deep stack is far larger than any single filter (a standard computation every student should be able to do, including the dilated version). Key operations to master: strided convolution versus pooling (learned downsampling versus fixed), padding conventions (valid/full/same and framework off-by-one in output size formulas), 1x1 'projection' convolutions for channel mixing and bottleneck cost reduction, and the efficient variants that decouple cost from channel count: grouped convolution (split channels, reduce MACs by group factor; used by ResNeXt with cardinality), depthwise separable convolution (one filter per channel plus a 1x1 pointwise, cutting cost by ~1/k^2 + 1/C_out - the basis of MobileNet, whose inverted residual block with linear bottleneck reorders expansion and depthwise steps), dilated/atrous convolution (exponentially growing field with no resolution loss, for segmentation), deformable convolution (learned sampling offsets), and asymmetric/shift-based cheap spatial mixing. The lineage is conceptually simple and worth teaching as an argument about depth: LeNet (hand-tuned small convnets) to AlexNet (GPUs, ReLU, dropout, overlapping pooling, data augmentation) to VGG (3x3 stacking, uniformity, depth by repetition) to NiN (1x1 as MLP) to GoogLeNet/Inception (parallel multi-scale branches plus factorized bottlenecks to buy depth cheaply) to ResNet (skip connections: depth 152 trained because gradients had an identity path, plus bottleneck design and the observation that residual nets are ensembles of variable-length paths) to DenseNet (dense feature reuse, memory cost) to NASNet/EfficientNet (compound scaling of depth/width/resolution under a resource budget, replacing hand design with search plus a scaling law) to ConvNeXt (showing a pure-convolutional stage design, with modern training recipes - GELU, large kernels, AdamW, mixup - matches ViT performance, i.e. much of ViT's advantage was training, not architecture) and finally the 'ReLU-free' line (RepVGG reparameterizes a multi-branch residual training graph into a plain VGG-like inference graph, showing branch structure can be moved into training and removed at inference; spatially selective convolutions in ConvNeXt V2 similarly restore gating behavior in a conv backbone). The lesson a learner should take: convolutional design is a repeated negotiation among receptive field, parameter/compute budget, gradient path, and trainability - and recipe changes are as consequential as topology changes.

topics.name: Recurrent Networks, LSTM, GRU, and Sequence-to-Sequence
topics.definition: Recurrent networks share one transition function across time (h_t = f(h_{t-1}, x_t)); LSTM and GRU add multiplicative gates that create persistent additive state paths; sequence-to-sequence models attach an attention-bearing decoder to an encoder so the output length need not match the input.
topics.explanation: A vanilla RNN computes a fixed-point-like trajectory h_t = tanh(W_hh h_{t-1} + W_xh x_t + b), whose training signal for step t-k is multiplied by k Jacobians W_hh diag(tanh'), so unless the spectral radius of W_hh is tuned to lie near 1 with non-saturating directions, long-range credit assignment either vanishes or explodes; this is why BPTT with truncated windows, and echo-state/'slow' recurrent dynamics, were the classical mitigations. Hochreiter and Schmidhuber's LSTM answers with a cell state updated as c_t = f_t * c_{t-1} + i_t * g_t: because the forget gate can hold at 1, the gradient path is an additive identity (a learned residual connection, as Gers, Schmidhuber and Cummins later made explicit and as modern analyses emphasize), so error can flow across hundreds of steps without saturation; the input/output gates modulate writing and reading, giving an approximately gated linear dynamical system. The GRU merges the two states into a single hidden state with an update gate and reset gate - one fewer multiplicative gate, comparable performance, less memory. Sequence-to-sequence (Sutskever et al. 2014) fixed the fixed-length, single-vector bottleneck of encoder-decoder RNNs: encode x into a state sequence, then decode y_t from an autoregressive state attending over the encoder states. Bahdanau's additive attention was introduced precisely because a single context vector degrades with input length, and it also fixes the alignment problem in translation; attention is simultaneously (i) a differentiable content-based lookup, (ii) a soft alignment that made neural MT competitive with statistical MT, and (iii) an interpretable diagnostic (which caveat: alignment visualizations are not alignments in the linguistic sense). Worth teaching for continuity, not history: RNNs remain the right tool for streaming/online state and constant-memory inference (KV-cache grows linearly in transformers whereas RNN state is fixed), LSTM/GRU cells appear as the recurrent core of gating-based models such as RWKV, and modern deep-recurrence work (layer-stacked LSTMs, residual RNNs) shows recurrent models still win on some sequential-signal and time-series tasks.

topics.name: Attention Mechanics: Scaled Dot-Product, Multi-Head, Masking, and the KV-Cache
topics.definition: Attention computes, for each query, a convex combination of value vectors whose weights are softmax of query-key dot products scaled by 1/sqrt(d_k); multi-head runs this in parallel subspaces, causal masks enforce autoregressive factorization, and the KV-cache stores past key/value projections so incremental decoding is linear rather than quadratic.
topics.explanation: The formula Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QK^T/sqrt(d_k))V has three reasons behind each element that courses routinely under-explain. (1) The scaling: if query and key components are roughly independent with unit variance, q.k has variance d_k, so logits grow like sqrt(d_k); unscaled softmax saturates toward one-hot as d_k grows, whose Jacobian collapses (softmax' = diag(p)-pp^T vanishes when p is extreme) and gradient dies - dividing by sqrt(d_k) keeps logit variance O(1). (2) Softmax as a differentiable max with temperature: entropy of attention rows is the temperature's shadow, and large-norm weights, low entropy, and long sequences interact, which is why entropy/attention-collapse regularization and logit soft-capping appear in production models. (3) The complexity and memory: the attention matrix is n x n per head, so training cost and inference memory scale quadratically in length; the exact algorithm (FlashAttention) recomputes rather than materializes that matrix by tiling and online-softmax rescaling, giving identical results with IO-bound cost O(n^2 d / M) instead of O(n^2) HBM traffic. Masking must be understood as additive -inf (or large negative) logits before softmax; a causal mask makes row i depend only on j <= i, which is what makes the model's factorization prod_t p(x_t | x_<t) exact rather than an approximation, and cross-attention masks (padding, look-ahead, prefix) are the same operation over a different axis. Multi-head is not 'more attention' in a naive sense: with d_model = h d_k, each head is a learned low-rank bilinear form in a subspace, so heads specialize in different relation types and, crucially, the model can mix local, syntactic, and positional behaviors that a single full-rank form cannot represent simultaneously. The inference-time machinery is the part most curricula omit: an autoregressive decoder at step t recomputes only x_t, but must attend to all previous positions, so the K/V projections of previous tokens are cached (KV-cache), making per-step compute O(n d) and memory O(2 h d_k n b) - which for long contexts and large batch dominates weight memory. Hence MQA (shared K/V across heads), GQA (grouped sharing), multi-token/Sliding-window variants, KV quantization and eviction policies, paged attention for memory fragmentation, and prefill/decode split serving. Understanding KV-cache is what makes the differences between GPT-style inference cost, streaming, and recurrent models legible.

topics.name: Transformer Block Internals: Normalization Placement, MLP Blocks, and Stacking Conventions
topics.definition: Beyond the attention equation, a working Transformer is a choice of block recipe - where normalization sits (post-norm vs pre-norm vs sandwich/DeepNorm), how the positionwise MLP is shaped (GELU two-layer vs gated GLU variants), how layers are stacked and initialized, and where biases/tying/residual scaling go.
topics.explanation: The original encoder block x + LN(x + Attn(x)) is post-norm: normalization follows the residual add, which produces well-scaled activations but forces the residual stream to be renormalized every layer, so the identity path is not preserved and gradient norms at the input grow with depth - empirically the reason post-norm Transformers need careful warmup and rarely scale past tens of layers. Pre-norm x + Attn(LN(x)) makes each block a small perturbation of the residual stream (a near-identity map whose norm grows additively rather than multiplicatively), which is why it trains to hundreds of layers with no warmup gymnastics; the known costs are that later layers see a residual stream whose norm grew (so their relative contribution shrinks - 'residual stream dilution'), that the final output needs an extra normalization, and that representation norm can grow unchecked, motivating per-layer learnable scaling (LayerScale), DeepNorm's fixed alpha/beta pairing to bound depth-rescaling, or normalization-free variants that use scaled tanh or QK-norm to control logits. The MLP block is the other half and is often glossed: a positionwise two-layer network with 4x expansion, whose parameters are typically 2/3 of the block, so the FFN - not attention - carries most of the model's memory/capacity; this is why gated variants (GEGLU, SwiGLU, with 2/3-scaled hidden width to hold parameter count fixed) outperform plain GELU MLPs, why GLU's multiplicative gating is the LLM default, and why MoE replaces this FFN. Practical conventions to know: attention/FFN alternation with shared residual stream, QK-LayerNorm in ViT/CoCa-style models to bound logit scale, weight tying between embedding and unembedding (which interacts with logit magnitude and label smoothing), dropout locations (post-residual vs inside attention vs MLP), no bias in projection layers when followed by LayerNorm (the bias is absorbed), and initialization of residual outputs near zero. A student should be able to read any model config (pre/post-norm, activation, expansion ratio, tie_word_embeddings) and predict trainability, parameter allocation, and rough memory.

topics.name: Positional Encoding Mathematics: Sinusoidal, Learned, RoPE, ALiBi, and Long Context
topics.definition: Because attention is permutation equivariant, order must be injected explicitly: either into the token representations (sinusoidal, learned embeddings) or into the attention logits themselves (RoPE's rotary relative dot product, ALiBi's linear relative bias, or NoPE where causality alone induces order).
topics.explanation: Self-attention satisfies Attention(P X) = P Attention(X) for a permutation P of positions, so an architecture with only content-based logits cannot distinguish 'dog bites man' from 'man bites dog'. Vaswani's sinusoidal encoding PE(pos, 2i) = sin(pos / 10000^{2i/d}) is a set of geometrically spaced frequencies; the identity PE(pos+k) = R_k PE(pos) with a rotation matrix makes inner products a function of relative offset, and the Fourier-basis view (a low-dimensional embedding of the cyclic group) explains both extrapolation behavior and the sensitivity to frequency coverage. Learned absolute embeddings are simpler and usually better in-domain but memorize positions, which is why they extrapolate poorly and waste embedding parameters. Attention with Linear BIas (ALiBi) skips input-side position information entirely and adds -h_m * |i-j| to the logits with head-specific slopes forming a harmonic-like sequence, which is monotone recency bias with zero extra parameters and demonstrated strong length extrapolation (a 512-token-trained model usable at thousands) - and it composes with causal masking trivially. RoPE rotates the query and key vectors in 2D coordinate pairs by angle pos * theta_i, so the dot product becomes a function of (i-j) times the content, preserving locality while leaving values untouched; because it is applied inside attention it has become the LLM default, and its generalization is exactly a complex-multiplication structure on the bilinear form - practical consequences include per-dimension frequency choice (base scaling, NTK-aware scaling, and YaRN, which interpolates/reshapes frequencies to extend context), the interaction with attention entropy and with logit capping, and the fact that RoPE alone gives limited extrapolation (it needs explicit frequency rescaling to stretch). NoPE - omitting position encodings in causal decoders - empirically still learns ordering because the autoregressive mask makes position implicit in the trajectory, an instructive result for separating 'position information' from 'position parameters'. At the system level long context is architectural, not just positional: sliding-window/local attention and its hierarchical variants, StreamingLLM's attention sinks (a few initial keys/values stabilize the recurrence, revealing a softmax normalization artifact), Ring/distributed attention for cross-device context, KV-cache compression (quantized, evicted, merged tokens), retrieval as an alternative to in-window memory, and the measured fact that long-context quality is dominated by effective attention over long ranges (position-interpolation fine-tuning) rather than by the encoding scheme alone.

topics.name: Sub-Quadratic Attention: Sparsemax, Linear Attention, and Structured Sparsity
topics.definition: Attention variants that reduce the O(n^2) cost or the softmax's dense convex-combination behavior: sparse-prototype classifiers such as sparsemax and entmax (sparse attention weights), kernelized/linear attention that avoids the n x n matrix entirely, block/local/global patterns, and low-rank approximations.
topics.explanation: Softmax returns strictly positive weights on all keys, which costs O(n^2) compute and memory and gives a diffuse, hard-to-interpret mixture. Martins and Astudillo's sparsemax is the Euclidean projection of the score vector onto the probability simplex: unlike softmax it can produce exact zeros and it has a well-defined sparse support, with a closed-form solution via a threshold (sort, cumulative sums, find the support) and gradients that propagate only through the support, and entmax (alpha-entmax, including the 1.5 case) generalizes this with a tunable sparsity level from sparsemax (alpha=1) to softmax (alpha=0). Sparse attention based on entmax was the first demonstration that trainable sparse attention can match softmax attention on seq2seq while yielding interpretable hard alignments - the important conceptual point being that the choice of regularizer in the max-entropy/optimization view (negative entropy gives softmax, squared-norm gives sparsemax) determines attention's sparsity, and that sparsemax's finite-support property means a query can attend to nothing rather than to everything weakly. The other axis is asymptotics: linear attention rewrites softmax-free attention as a matrix product associative trick - given features phi(q), phi(k), compute phi(Q)(phi(K)^T V) so cost is O(n d^2) with O(d^2) state, at the price of dropping the query-key interaction's exact renormalization; Katharopoulos' Performer approximates softmax by random-feature kernel maps (with the unbounded-positive-output caveat), and modern state-space models are best understood as the same algebra (see the SSM topic and structured state space duality). Beyond these: fixed-pattern locality (sliding window, block-sparse BigBird with random/global blocks), content-based sparsity (Reformer's LSH buckets, which are nondifferentiable and hurt recall), and dynamic/token-pruning approaches. A learner should be able to say precisely what is being traded: exactness of the convex combination, sparsity/interpretability, gradient quality, hardware-friendliness (dense GEMMs beat clever sparse patterns on GPUs), and whether the memory state is bounded - which is why sub-quadratic attention is a hardware story as much as a math story, and why the practical winner at scale has mostly been 'keep softmax, make it IO-efficient' (FlashAttention) plus context-level tricks.

topics.name: State-Space Models: S4, Selective SSMs (Mamba), RWKV, and Hybrids
topics.definition: State-space models compute a linear recurrence h_t = A h_{t-1} + B x_t, y_t = C h_t whose discretized convolution form makes training parallel (O(n log n) via FFT) while inference is constant-memory; SSMs are the modern synthesis of recurrent efficiency and transformer-scale trainability.
topics.explanation: Continuous-time SSMs (x' = Ax + Bu, y = Cx) discretized with a step Delta give h_t = Abar h_{t-1} + Bbar u_t, which unrolled is a linear time-invariant convolution with kernel K = (C B, C A B, C A^2 B, ...). The trick of S4 (Gu, Goel, Re) was to parameterize A as a normal matrix (a diagonal of complex-conjugate scales/angles, i.e. a HiPPO-style initialization approximating the Legendre memory polynomial operator so the state maintains a maximal-memory projection of the past) and to compute the kernel in the frequency domain, so training is a parallel FFT convolution while inference remains an O(1)-per-step recurrence. The limitation of LTI SSMs is that a fixed kernel cannot be input-dependent, so they cannot do selection/copying tasks well (prompt tuning, in-context retrieval), which drove the 'SSMs are not transformers' debate. Mamba (Gu and Dao) removes the LTI restriction: Delta, B, C are produced from the input, making the recurrence input-dependent and enabling content-based memory, and it introduces a hardware-aware selective scan that computes the non-parallel recurrence in chunks with recomputation, plus a purely recurrent (no attention, no MLP-expansion) residual architecture that gives linear scaling in length and constant-memory inference. Mamba-2 / structured state space duality (Dao and Gu) is the theoretically important part: with scalar-per-channel A, the recurrence's output equals a semiseparable-matrix form of attention, giving a precise bridge where transformer attention and SSMs are the same computation restricted differently - this explains linear attention, gated attention, and RWKV as points in one design space, and yields state-space duality: parallel training with attention-like matrices and recurrent inference. RWKV is the RNN-for-Large-Language-Models line: token-shift mixing plus an exponential-decay linear attention ('WKV' as a softmax-free attention with data-dependent keys), trained like a transformer, inferenced like an RNN, with time-mixing/channel-mixing blocks; it is a useful existence proof that sub-quadratic recurrent models can be made at LLM scale. Current practical picture: hybrids (attention every k layers, or Mamba-plus-attention stacks) retain in-context retrieval ability while cutting memory; selective-SSM vision backbones compete on dense prediction; and honest limits must be taught - pure SSMs still underperform transformers on long-context retrieval/copying, and the theory is young enough that 'constant memory' claims depend on implementation.

topics.name: Vision Transformers and Convolution-Attention Hybrids
topics.definition: A Vision Transformer patchifies an image into a sequence of embedding vectors, adds positional information, and applies a standard transformer encoder; hybrids replace, augment, or constrain attention with convolutional local processing.
topics.explanation: ViT's contribution was mostly a claim about data and training rather than about new layers: images become 16x16-patch tokens with a linear projection, plus a class token and 2D positions, and the transformer does the rest. Its consequences are exactly the things a student should be able to reason about. Attention has no built-in locality or translation prior and a low inductive bias, so ViTs underperform convnets on small data (ImageNet-size) but surpass them when pretrained at scale or with strong augmentation/distillation - the empirical result that 'scale can substitute for inductive bias'. Positional information in vision is a design surface: learned absolute embeddings, 2D-interpolated sinusoidal embeddings when resolution changes (needed for high-resolution fine-tuning and for any variable input size), relative-position biases, factorized 2D RoPE, and coordinate-aware variants (CoordMamba-style) all trade extrapolation for parameter cost. Global attention is also expensive at image resolution: with (HW/p^2) tokens, quadratic cost is why local/window attention (Swin's shifted windows with no-shift on odd layers giving cross-window flow, with relative position bias and a hierarchical pyramid for dense prediction), axial/factorized attention (Axial-DeepLab, Swin-UNet style), downsampled-token attention (Pyramid ViT), and token reduction/pruning all exist. The hybrid space is where the argument settled: CoaT/BoTNet/CvT/LeViT mix conv-local and attention-global layers; MobileViT trades the tradeoff for on-device use; and the ConvNeXt result (a pure convnet reaching ViT parity with modern recipe) plus the ViT-22B scaling analysis together say the layer type matters less than the training recipe, resolution schedule, and compute allocation, while MAE-style masked reconstruction plus self-attention is where transformers clearly help vision (an architecture-agnostic objective that attention makes easy). Also teach: hierarchical vs plain design (dense tasks need multi-scale feature maps), class-token vs global-average-pooling readout, attention as pooling (attention pooling, Perceiver-style latent arrays as a general resolution-agnostic bottleneck), and how ViT is the backbone of CLIP/DINOv2/SAM, so patch/embedding conventions determine what those systems can see.

topics.name: Graph Neural Networks: Message Passing, Aggregation, and Expressiveness Limits
topics.definition: A GNN computes node features by iterating a local update in which each node aggregates transformed features of its neighbors (message passing); the learnable components are the message function, the aggregation, and the readout, and the model class is bounded by the Weisfeiler-Lehman test of graph isomorphism.
topics.explanation: The standard framework (Gilmer et al.'s MPNN, Bronstein et al.'s formulation) is x_i' = gamma( x_i, rho( { (phi(x_i, x_j), x_e) : j in N(i) } ) ): permutation-invariant aggregation (sum, mean, max - the DeepSets theorem says mean-sum type aggregation with enough width approximates multiset functions) composed with learned transformations, which makes GNNs equivariant on the graph and permutation-invariant at the graph readout level. GCN is the first-order localized Chebyshev/spectral approximation: it normalizes the adjacency as D^{-1/2}(A+I)D^{-1/2} and propagates features, an approximation that is cheap and works but is only a linear filter bank in graph structure, with the constraint that self-loops and symmetric normalization matter (removing them changes spectrum). GAT replaces fixed normalization with learned attention over neighbors, giving data-dependent weights; GraphSAGE samples and aggregates neighbors inductively for large graphs, which is what makes production recommendation/graph systems feasible. Three structural limits define the theory. (1) Expressiveness: the Weisfeiler-Lehman hierarchy - message-passing GNNs are at most as discriminating as 1-WL, so they cannot distinguish regular graphs of the same degree profile, cannot count triangles/substructures, and (Morris et al., Maron et al.) higher-order GNNs correspond to k-WL while subgraph-structure-aware designs (ES-GNN, PNA's degree/bonding centrality scalers, ID incorporation) buy power at extra cost; k-WL equivalence does not mean identical function classes but means the same discrimination ceiling. (2) Depth: repeated smoothing causes oversmoothing - the features converge to a common low-dimensional subspace (signal decays toward the dominant eigenvector; provably in linear models, empirically in deep ones), which motivates JK-net/readout-from-all-layers, residual connections (the same story as ResNet), PairNorm/differentially-private rescaling, and oversquashing in the gradient path (information-theoretic bottleneck along graph curvature, Türe et al.'s argument). (3) Heterophily: aggregation assumes neighbors are similar; on graphs where they are not, designs must separate ego- and neighbor-embedding or use higher-order structure. Graph transformers answer the 'attention can be exact' question by adding positional/structural encodings (random-walk, Laplacian eigenvector, distance) so that full attention over nodes is not permutation-invariant-degenerate - but they pay O(N^2) in node count and need careful sampling/sparsification for large graphs. Include the practical vocabulary: node/graph/link-level tasks, mini-batching by neighborhood sampling, and inductive generalization to unseen graphs, plus honest open problems (there is no accepted notion of 'graph depth limit', benchmarks leak into architecture design, and expressiveness theory is a statement about distinguishability, not learnability).

topics.name: Neural Operators: Learning Maps Between Function Spaces
topics.definition: A neural operator learns a mapping between infinite-dimensional function spaces (e.g. a PDE coefficient field to its solution field) that is discretization-consistent: it takes functions as input and outputs functions, approximated at any resolution by point evaluations.
topics.explanation: Standard surrogate modeling trains a network on a fixed grid, so its prediction quality degrades when the grid changes; a neural operator is designed so that resolution affects only the number of evaluations, not the parameterization. DeepONet (Lu, Jagtap, Karniadakis) writes the operator as G(u)(y) = sum_k r_k(v_1,...,v_m)(u) * b_k(y): a branch net that reads a finite set of evaluations of the input function and produces coefficients, and a trunk net that evaluates basis functions at the output query point y - which is universal in the sense of an approximated sum-separable tensor representation, and cheap for arbitrary output points. The Fourier Neural Operator (Li, Kovachki, Azizzadenesheli et al.) replaces the layer's integral kernel with a global convolution implemented in Fourier space: for each mode retained, a learned linear transform multiplies the truncated spectral coefficients, i.e. W_eff = R^{-1} (P) R restricted to k_max modes, giving an O(N log N) global receptive field whose support is resolution-independent. The crucial theoretical property to teach is discretization convergence (FNO and graph kernels are discretization-consistent; approximation results bound the error as a function of grid refinement, which is what a numerical-analysis audience demands), and the design implications: channel lifting/projection, spectral truncation as a low-pass prior (explaining why FNO captures coarse dynamics and struggles with sharp discontinuities unless modes are increased), pointwise nonlinearities between spectral convolutions, and the alternative of kernel-integral (Ginstra-Brand-style) or message-passing-on-point-clouds operators for irregular geometry. Scientific-ML context: operators are used as differentiable surrogates inside inverse problems and control, for turbulence/CFD closure, weather/emulation of dynamical models where equivariance and conservation laws must be built in (equivariant and conservative architectures, neural conservation laws), and as components where PDE solving is done by implicit-neural-VMC or PINN-like residual losses - the distinction between operator learning (supervised map), PINN (physics residual as loss), and mesh-based GNNs is a common exam question. Honest gaps: data cost for high-fidelity PDE datasets, generalization across PDE parameters is not guaranteed, and spectral truncation is a modeling assumption that fails on non-periodic/sharp phenomena (windowing, multi-resolution FNO, wavelet operators address this).

topics.name: Mixture-of-Experts and Sparse Computation
topics.definition: A mixture-of-experts replaces a dense layer with N parallel expert networks plus a learned router that sends each token to a small subset of experts, so parameters grow while per-token FLOPs stay roughly constant.
topics.explanation: Shazeer et al.'s originally noisy-top-k formulation (add learned Gaussian noise to the gating logits, keep top-k, differentiate through a softmax over the selected set) became Switch Transformer (top-1 routing, which cuts routing compute and simplifies sharding) and GShard (top-2 with capacity factor). Every design question is a load-balancing question: routers collapse to using a few experts unless (a) an auxiliary balance loss (Switch's fraction-of-tokens-to-expert term) or expert-bias adjustment (ST-MoE's free load-balancing via a bias term that changes routing but not the gradient) is added, and (b) a capacity factor bounds tokens per expert so the fixed-shape tensors required by distributed hardware do not drop tokens - dropped-token handling is a real correctness issue. The engineering core: experts are placed across devices with all-to-all communication, so throughput is set by network topology, and per-expert FFN width, expert granularity (fine-grained experts with shared/fixed experts, as in DeepSeek-MoE), and routing level (per-layer, per-token, or finer) determine quality per FLOP. What MoE actually buys is capacity without inference cost - the reason it dominates frontier-scale language models and multimodal models - and what it costs: memory for all experts at inference (or expert offloading/quantization), unstable training at scale (router drift, expert specialization collapse), and difficult knowledge-localization interpretation; 'the model has 671B parameters but 37B active' is a statement about FLOPs, not about memory or data requirements, which is a common misreading. Extend to non-LLM sparse computation as the same idea: dynamic routing (capsules), conditional computation by early exit or depth adaptivity, expert dropout, and MoE layers inside diffusion transformers (which is how DiT-style models scale generative capacity per step).

topics.name: Neural Architecture Search: Meta-Learning, DARTS, Weight Sharing, and LLM-Driven Search
topics.definition: Neural architecture search automates the design of a network's topology and hyperparameters by searching over a space of candidate architectures with an evaluator, using reinforcement learning or meta-learning, differentiable relaxation, one-shot weight sharing, or proposal generation by an LLM.
topics.explanation: Early NAS (Zoph and Le 2016) used an RL controller emitting a description, with the child trained and its validation accuracy as reward - correct but absurdly expensive, which motivated the two efficiency ideas that define the field. First, transfer/meta-learning of architecture quality: the 'predictor' and 'one-shot' lines train a supernet once and evaluate many sub-networks by reusing its shared weights, which is the basis of ENAS (RNN controller over a shared-weight cell space) and of OFA (once-for-all, elastic kernels/depth/width with a post-training specialization pass and, importantly, a fair-evolutionary search over the trained supernet). Second, differentiable relaxation: DARTS converts the discrete choice 'which operation on which edge' into a mixture alpha_e * sum_o w_o(x), optimizes architecture parameters alpha jointly with weights by gradient (bilevel optimization), then discretizes by keeping the largest alphas - and its known pathology is that the relaxed optimum is a bad proxy for the discrete one (PC-DARTS, PDARTS, and studies of the DARTS 'collapse to skip connections' failure exist because of this), so the field's honest summary is that relaxation gives cheap searches with reproducibility problems. Weight-sharing searches have their own statistical subtlety: subnets within a supernet differ in weight initialization and training length, so rankings can be dominated by weight inheritance rather than topology (this is the 'search space and ranking' critique of EfficientNet-era work). Third, LLM-driven and quality-diversity search: evolutionary/quality-diversity methods (NEAT, omni-QD, MAP-Elites) and LLMs that propose code-level architectures or act as mutation operators, plus cost-aware multi-objective search over latency/memory, are the current frontier - they help because the search space can be expressed as constrained code and because the objective includes hardware metrics that hand-designed spaces ignore. The critical evaluation questions: how is compute counted (search budget vs final training budget), is the search fair, and does the found architecture beat human designs under matched budget? Also teach the transfer result that NAS cells are dataset-agnostic but not task-agnostic, and the sobering point that in most deployed systems, hand-designed architectures plus better recipes win - so NAS is best framed as a tool for hardware-constrained specialization, not a replacement for architectural understanding.

topics.name: The Diffusion Transformer (DiT) and Token-Based Generative Backbones
topics.definition: A diffusion transformer is a transformer denoiser that predicts the noise (or velocity) of latent patches conditioned on timestep and label, replacing the U-Net convolutional backbone that dominated latent diffusion, with conditioning injected by adaptive normalization, in-context tokens, or cross-attention.
topics.explanation: Peebles and Xie's DiT showed that the denoising network's architecture was not the bottleneck: patchify the VAE latent into tokens, run a plain transformer block, and condition on t and class via adaLN-Zero, where the modulation parameters (shift/scale on the normalized activations and the output gate) are produced by a small MLP of the conditioning signal with zero-initialized gates so each block starts as identity - which is the residual-scaling argument from the Transformer internals topic applied to generative training. Two findings matter for scaling: representation quality (self-attention over tokens versus convolutional locality) is largely irrelevant at sufficient compute, while model size measured by Gflops correlates monotonically with generative quality (FID) - a transformer-style scaling law for generation, and the reason modern image and video generators (Sora-class, most frontier text-to-image models) are DiT-based. Conditioning mechanisms are the design surface: adaLN(-Zero) is cheap but couples all tokens to one global signal, cross-attention (as in Stable Diffusion's text conditioning, which requires a separate conditioning pathway and more parameters) allows spatially varying conditioning, and in-context conditioning (concatenating tokens) is used for reference images/editing and for classifier-free guidance bookkeeping. Timestep embedding itself is a positional-encoding problem: t is embedded with sinusoidal features (the same Fourier-features logic as positional encodings) so the network can resolve high-frequency noise-level dependence - and its sensitivity explains why noise-schedule and timestep-embedding choices interact. Video generative versions add spatiotemporal factorized attention (space then time blocks or full 3D attention), which is where compute actually blows up, plus 3D VAE tokenization. The architectural takeaways to teach: the generative model's backbone obeys the same pre-norm/residual/MoE design rules as LLMs; token resolution determines cost quadratically; and scaling generative quality is primarily a compute/data/parameter matter rather than a topology invention - which is precisely the claim the DiT paper provides evidence for, and the reason it is a curricular landmark. Honest limits: FID-vs-Gflops monotonicity is a coarse quality proxy (see generative evaluation), and DiT does not address sampling cost per step or distillation, which is where subsequent work concentrated.

topics.name: Spiking, Capsule, Liquid, Memory-Augmented, and World-Model Architectures
topics.definition: A family of architectures that each reject one mainstream assumption - continuous different activations (spiking), scalar per-unit features (capsules), fixed time constants (liquid networks), state-only memory (external-memory networks), or direct policy learning (world models) - and pay for it with a harder optimization problem.
topics.explanation: Spiking networks propagate discrete events through leaky-integrate-and-fire dynamics (dv/dt = (input - (v - v_rest))/tau with threshold and reset), so information lives in spike timing and the network is asynchronous by construction; because spikes are nondifferentiable, learning uses surrogate gradients (a smooth kernel replacing the threshold derivative, now the standard and it trains deep SNNs), ANN-to-SNN conversion with discretization error bounds, or local STDP rules, and the reason the family survives is energy on event-driven hardware (Loihi-class chips) for sensing/streaming workloads - while the honest caveat is that SNNs still trail ANNs on static vision benchmarks, so accuracy and energy must not be conflated. Capsule networks (Hinton, Sabour) replace scalars with vectors whose length is an existence probability and whose orientation is pose, predicting a child capsule's pose by a learned transformation and coupling layers by dynamic routing-by-agreement, an EM-like iterative fixed point; what they recover is exactly what pooling destroys - the part-whole pose relationship - giving viewpoint and occlusion robustness on small data, and what stopped them scaling is slow unstable routing and fragile equivariance, since modern models buy the same robustness from data plus relative positional encodings. Liquid neural networks (Hasani et al.) are continuous-time recurrent cells whose time constants are functions of the input, so effective memory adapts online; their motivation is closed-loop control on real robots under unanticipated perturbation, and they sit technically between reservoir computing and neural ODEs. The memory-augmented lineage argues that a fixed-width hidden state must both represent and store, so an external matrix of slots with content-based addressing (NTM's key-query soft addressing with interpolation/sharpening, DNC's linked-list temporal addressing and usage-based allocation) gives near-unbounded, addressable storage with trained algorithms (copy, associative recall); the sober lesson is that these models were displaced not because memory was wrong but because a transformer's attention over context - and operationally its growing KV-cache - is a soft, differentiable, larger memory that trains far more easily, which is also why retrieval-augmented and kNN-augmented systems are the lineage's descendants. World models make the complementary move of learning the environment's latent dynamics so that prediction and control happen inside the model: Ha and Schmidhuber's VAE plus MDN-RNN, PlaNet's Recurrent State-Space Model (deterministic hidden state plus stochastic latent, trained by an ELBO with prior and posterior, planned against with MPPI-style sampling), and Dreamer/DreamerV3's imagined rollouts for policy and value learning; JEPA-style latent-predictive objectives port the same idea to representation learning by predicting a teacher's representation rather than pixels, so capacity is not spent on unpredictable detail. The shared open problems are real and worth stating plainly: compounding model error limits imagination horizons, memory capacity in learned systems remains far from what the addressability argument suggests, and biological plausibility or theoretical elegance has repeatedly failed to predict engineering adoption.

subdomains.name: Likelihood Objectives and Latent-Variable Models
subdomains.summary: What a generative model can be asked to do (density, sample, infer latents) and the objectives that trade these off: exact likelihood, ELBO bounds, and unnormalized energy.

topics.name: The Generative Model Landscape: Likelihood, ELBO Structure, and Energy-Based Objectives
topics.definition: Generative models are organized by what they make available - tractable exact likelihood, tractable sampling, an optimizing bound, or neither - and the four families (autoregressive/flow, latent-variable with an ELBO, adversarial, and energy-based) occupy different points in that trade space.
topics.explanation: The canonical 2x2 is (exact vs approximate likelihood) x (explicit vs implicit density), giving: autoregressive and normalizing-flow models with exact factorized or change-of-variable likelihoods; latent-variable models (VAE, GAN+latent, diffusion) that optimize a bound or none; adversarial/implicit models with sampling but no density; and energy-based models with an unnormalized density and hence no likelihood term at all. The ELBO is the load-bearing object: log p(x) = ELBO(q) + KL(q(z|x) || p(z|x)), so the gap is the posterior KL - a bound that is tight iff the variational posterior equals the true posterior - and every 'bound tightening' development is a way of shrinking that gap or of making the objective better suited to the task: importance-weighted bounds (IWAE tightens log p(x) as O(1/k) with k importance samples but does not improve the learned q's KL to posterior in the same way), amortized inference versus per-example optimization (VLAE), auxiliary/inverse autoregressive and masked-dependency variational posteriors to fix the posterior-collapse pathology, hierarchical/deterministic latents (VampPrior-style mixtures of posteriors, autoregressive priors), and discrete/annealed latents. Diffusion and flow-matching complicate the picture in a way students must handle precisely: with a variational bound written over the forward noise process, the ELBO becomes a weighted integral of denoising score-matching losses (Song et al.'s sufficient condition on the weighting) plus boundary terms, so a diffusion model is simultaneously a bound-optimizer and an implicit generator whose likelihood is computable only by an ODE/SDE probability-flow argument. Energy-based models are the complementary extreme: p(x) = exp(-E_theta(x))/Z, trained by pushing E down on data and up on samples obtained by MCMC (contrastive divergence, PC/CD in RBMs, long-run chains, NCE/Split-VSM as Z-free objectives, InfoNCE with an interpretable mutual-information lower bound); the partition function is intractable, so EBM training is a sampling problem in disguise - which explains both their flexibility (arbitrary unnormalized couplings, and a natural interpretation of diffusion as iterative energy descent, and adversarial-discriminator-as-energy) and their instability. A curriculum should also make the meta-point: likelihood is not the only quality criterion and can be actively misleading for perceptual tasks (ELBO values differ from log-likelihood in diffusion, and the field's post-2020 consensus is that likelihood and FID are weakly correlated), while 'fully tractable likelihood' remains essential for anomaly detection and for inference-time scoring - the topic that keeps generative modeling from being only about pictures.

Reasoning about model comparison beyond FID
common_misconceptions: A tighter ELBO always means a better model of the data (it changes the inference network and can just fit the bound better).
Variational lower bound equals log-likelihood (it is a bound; the gap is a posterior KL).
EBMs are likelihood-free because they are unnormalized, so they cannot be evaluated at all (they can be compared via metrics, but no density).
Diffusion models have no likelihood (they have an implicit one via the probability-flow ODE, hard to estimate tightly).

topics.name: Variational Autoencoders and Latent-Variable Modeling
topics.definition: A VAE is a generative model with a prior p(z), a decoder p_theta(x|z) and an amortized encoder q_phi(z|x), trained to maximize the evidence lower bound, with sampling performed by drawing z and passing it through the decoder.
topics.explanation: The reparameterization trick z = mu_phi(x) + sigma_phi(x) * eps with eps ~ N(0, I) is what makes the gradient of the bound low-variance and differentiable through the stochastic node; without it, the score-function (REINFORCE) estimator's variance makes training impractical, and this single change is the reason VAEs are trainable at all. The bound decomposes into a reconstruction term (cross-entropy for discrete or squared error up to a constant for Gaussian decoders) plus a regularizer KL(q(z|x) || p(z)) that pulls the aggregate posterior toward the prior, which is simultaneously the source of VAEs' virtues (a usable latent space, principled missing-data/semi-supervised extensions, interpolation, and an explicit information bottleneck) and their pathologies. Key ones to teach: posterior collapse, where KL terms go to zero for uninformative latents because the powerful decoder does not need them, mitigated by annealing the KL weight, latent-ordering tricks (KL-ball/total-correlation penalties, DNFi-style disentanglement, Variational RNN priors), and discrete-latent difficulty (the straight-through estimator's biased gradients, Gumbel-Softmax's relaxed-but-still-biased objective, and VQ's alternative of a hard codebook with an EMA update). Blur is a real limitation and it is not only about the objective: pixel-space decoders with per-pixel independent Gaussian/Laplacian likelihoods cannot model high-frequency structure well and the ELBO itself is a weak fit criterion for perceptual tasks; the field's fixes were to move diffusion into the decoder role (VDM, diffusion-decoder VAEs) and to accept that latent compression - not generative quality - is VAEs' durable contribution, which is why essentially every modern latent diffusion system uses a VAE (or VQGAN) tokenizer as its compression front end. Also worth stating: beta-VAE's hyperparameter makes the information bottleneck explicit and trades rate for distortion (a rate-distortion reading that is the honest way to describe disentanglement gains), and deterministic/discrete-latent variants are the standard tool in speech and audio tokenization where the codebook is the model.

Explain why reparameterization beats the score-function estimator here, with a variance argument.

Explain discrete-latent gradient problems (ST estimator bias, Gumbel-Softmax limitations, VQ alternatives).
Explain why pixel-space VAE samples look blurry and what the objective-vs-metric explanation is.

applications: Anomaly detection via reconstruction and KL
common_misconceptions: VAE blur proves the model class is weak (the ELBO plus per-pixel likelihood is the cause; the class is fine).
A smaller beta always improves generation (it trades rate for distortion and can cause collapse-free but unstructured latents).
Posterior collapse means the latent space is useless (only some dimensions collapse; it is measurable per dimension).

topics.name: GANs: Minimax Dynamics, WGAN Theory, and the StyleGAN Lineage
topics.definition: A GAN trains a generator against a discriminator in a two-player game; the original formulation minimizes a JS-divergence-like value function that provably reaches Nash equilibrium only if both players are optimal, and the practical lineage is a sequence of fixes to optimization, mode coverage, and controllability.
topics.explanation: Goodfellow et al.'s analysis is worth restating with its assumptions: with the discriminator able to reach its pointwise optimum D*(x) = p_data/(p_data + p_g), the generator's objective is monotone in JS(p_data || p_g), so minimizing it means matching the data distribution - but that inner maximization is exactly what SGD does not do, and the gradient of the generator loss near a well-fit discriminator vanishes, which is the theoretical root of mode collapse and training instability. Arjovsky et al.'s diagnosis is precise: if the data and generator supports are lower-dimensional, JS saturates and gives no gradient, while the Wasserstein-1 distance does; the critic must be 1-Lipschitz (enforced by weight clipping in WGAN, by a gradient penalty in WGAN-GP, or spectrally in SGAN/SNGAN), and this converts the game into a Kantorovich-Rubinstein dual, giving the meaningful statement 'minimize f-divergences only when supports overlap; otherwise use an integral probability metric'. That theory also explains the practical finding that critic regularization stabilizes GANs (a critic that generalizes is a critic whose gradient is informative), which the self-attention/projection-GAN line formalized as gradient regularization. The architecture lineage teaches something else: from DCGAN's convolutional stability rules (batchnorm in generator except output, strided downsampling, no fully-connected layers, LeakyReLU) through conditional GANs (auxiliary-classifier AC-GAN, class-conditional cGAN; later used for guidance), progressive growing (Karras et al. line) to StyleGAN's decisive idea - a learned per-style MLP mapping a latent z to a style vector w (which then drives per-layer affine modulation in a synthesis network) - which both made the latent space semantically traversable (interpolation, editing, and the famous w-space disentanglement, with the honest caveat that much of the observed effect is linear-structure in the trained generator rather than a property of the encoder) and fixed the 'water faucet' artifacts of earlier progressive nets by injecting noise per pixel and by removing the generator's direct view of z (the path length regularizer). StyleGAN2/3 added the R1 gradient penalty (finite-difference approximation is what most implementations actually use), the equalized-lr trick for Kaiming-without-init, and alias-free up/downsampling with filters, and StyleGAN3 made the generator approximately equivariant to translation by controlling aliasing in both sampling and nonlinearity - a rare case where the architecture is justified by signal-processing analysis rather than empiricism. Evaluation and modern status: GANs now mostly lose to diffusion on diversity/fidelity and coverage, but they win where single-step generation and cheap high-resolution synthesis matter (StyleGAN-based face/head avatars, image-to-image, super-resolution GANs, and GAN-inversion pipelines), and adversarial discriminators remain a component of latent tokenizers and 'adversarial + autoregressive' hybrids. Mode coverage must be discussed with the right metric (JSD is bad at it; see evaluation) and with the note that partial mode collapse is not detectable from a loss curve.
